text: A ski binding is a device that connects a ski boot to the ski. Before 1933, when ski lifts were introduced, skiers used the same gear for going uphill and downhill and for cross-country skiing. As ski lifts became more common, skis and their bindings became specialized, with distinctions emerging between alpine (downhill) and Nordic (cross-country, Telemark, and ski jumping) skiing. Until the mid-20th century, bindings held the toe of a flexible, leather boot against the ski and allowed the heel to rise off the ski, typically using a strap or cable around the heel. To reduce injuries from falls, ski bindings evolved to release the toe sideways in early models and forward and aft in later models. Downhill ski bindings became standardized for plastic ski boots and included a built-in brake that drags in the snow after the ski detaches from the boot. Cross-country ski bindings evolved from simple bent-metal plates with pins that held a square-toed leather boot toe under a wire bale to standardized systems that hold a plastic boot attached to a bar in a recess in the boot's toe. Back-country, jumping, and alpine touring ski bindings incorporate features from both alpine and Nordic bindings. Before the 1840s, ski bindings were leather straps fastened over the toe of the boot, similar to those used for snowshoes. Sondre Norheim demonstrated telemark skiing before 1866 and performed the Open Christiania turn in 1868, both made possible by a binding design from the late 1840s that included a loop of twisted birch roots running from the toe loops around the boot heels and back, allowing the heel to lift for walking and gliding while better holding the boot to the ski for greater control, replacing the use of large poles to drag the skier. Starting in 1894, Fritz R. Huitfeldt invented a binding with a secure toe iron that allowed the heel to move freely, which evolved through the 1930s as the standard design. Skiers who wanted to attach their heel to the ski used a "long-thong" strap. Further innovations included the Rottefella binding, developed in 1927 by Bror With, where "Rottefella" means "rat trap" in Norwegian; it featured a bent, pressed-metal plate with three or four pins that inserted into the toe of a square-toed boot, clamped down with a metal bail. After winning at the 1928 Winter Olympics in St. Moritz, the binding remained the standard for cross-country skiing for much of the century and continues as the Nordic Norm, manufactured by Rottefella and others. The cable binding enabled the Christie turn to become standard on downhill runs, and in 1929, Swiss racer Guido Reuge invented a cable binding with steel clips below the boot heel to clamp the heel down for downhill skiing, naming it "Kandahar" for the international Kandahar Cup races. In alpine races, the Kandahar binding caused serious leg injuries, leading to experimentation on fall-releasing bindings beginning in 1939. Hjalmar Hvam broke his leg skiing and, while recovering from surgery, invented the Saf-Ski toe binding in 1937, later selling it under the slogan "Hvoom with Hvam"; it was a metal clip with a pyramidal top that fit into a slot in the ski boot sole, allowing the toe to release when the boot rotated forward. The system was met with skepticism by professional skiers, especially when Olaf Rodegaard released during a race, though he credited it with saving him from a broken leg. Hvam sold several thousand pairs of Saf-Skis in the post-war era when alpine skiing was emerging, continuing to sell them into the 1960s, but in 1966 his insurance rates increased so much that he was forced out of the market. The Look Nevada, introduced in 1950, was a significant advancement, holding the toe centered over the ski with two metal fingers shaped like an upside-down V, pivoted to allow side motion and centered by a spring; during a fall, sideways torsion could overcome the spring force and allow the boot to release to the side. This design was quickly copied by others, notably Marker, and by the late 1950s, there were about 35 different release toe bindings on the US market, most using a normal Kandahar-style heel cable. The first modern heel-and-toe binding for alpine skiing was the Cubco, introduced in 1950 but not widely adopted until about 1960; it solved the problem of no heel attachment point by screwing small metal clips into the boot sole, eliminating performance changes due to boot wear or sole geometry. Marker introduced the Rotomat, which gripped the sole extending past the heel, and Look followed with the Grand Prix design. By the mid-1960s, release bindings working on both heel and toe were common, and by the late 1960s, cable bindings disappeared from alpine skiing. A problem with 1960s release bindings was that boots were not standardized, so a binding effective on one boot might be dangerous on another or become dangerous as the boot wore. This led to plate bindings, which used a metal plate clipped to the boot sole and bindings that clamped onto the plate, allowing easy removal for walking; these were popular in the US in the 1970s, notably the BURT Retractable Bindings and Spademan binding, but never gained traction in Europe. As European companies dominated the alpine skiing market, plate bindings disappeared despite excellent safety records. The decline was due to the introduction of standardized hard plastic boots, first introduced by Lange to improve leather designs; as plastic spread, the sole became standardized to allow toe-and-heel bindings to clip on. Plastic offered advantages over leather—being firmer, not deforming over time, and having predictable friction in wet or dry conditions—allowing easy adaptation to any ski for any skier. Injury rates in alpine skiing began to fall with the introduction of the Teflon anti-friction pad around 1972. Alpine ski bindings have two functions: retaining the boot on the ski and releasing it in a fall to prevent injury. Retention involves stepping into the binding toe-first and pressing down with the heel, causing a latch to engage the heel. Release occurs along two axes: forward and backward along the ski and torsionally, rotating over the top of the ski. Bindings allow a certain amount of boot flexure before releasing under pressure during a fall. Each binding is set for a DIN value based on the skier’s height, weight, age, and ability (rated from one for beginner to three for advanced). A snow brake prevents the ski from moving when not attached to a boot. Major manufacturers of alpine ski bindings include those listed. Alpine touring (or randonee) bindings allow the heel to be free and the toe in the binding when using Nordic techniques for ski touring, and both heel and toe in the binding when using alpine techniques to descend. Most touring bindings are designed for boots meeting one of two ISO specifications: "Tech" bindings use pins to hold the toe down and engage with the heel in downhill mode, with about 50% of ski boots having the necessary inserts; "Frame" bindings function like regular alpine bindings, gripping a welt in the heel. Manufacturers of alpine touring bindings include Atomic/Salomon, Black Diamond, Dynafit, Fritschi, Genuine Guide Gear, and Marker. Starting in the latter half of the 20th century, three standards emerged for cross-country and telemark bindings: the 75-mm Nordic Norm (NN), the Salomon Nordic System (SNS), and the New Nordic Norm (NNN). Ski jumping bindings are specialized and attach to the toe of square-toed plastic boots extending above the ankles, allowing the heel to rise and releasing in a fall. Companies that manufacture Nordic bindings include Alpina, Fischer, Madshus, Rossignol, and Rottefella. In 1975, Adidas explored an alternative to the Nordic Norm with a tab on the boot clamped in a narrow plastic binding. Salomon produced a boot with a metal loop protruding from the toe, clamped in its binding, followed by the 1979 Salomon Nordic System binding, which attached to a bar in a slot in the toe of the ski boot. This was emulated by Rottefella and others as the New Nordic Norm. Flexible plastics in boot soles allowed strength in torsion and side-to-side movement while retaining lengthwise flexibility and enabling heel lift without a heel cable. The Rottefella binding became standardized as the 75-mm, three-pin, Nordic Norm binding, widespread by the 1970s. The Salomon Nordic System (SNS) was the first integrated boot-binding system for cross-country skiing, followed by the New Nordic Norm. First-generation SNS used a looped bar in the boot sole; later generations engaged a bar recessed in the toe and included a single thick ridge on the binding plate. Variants included Pilot and Profil, with Pilot boots usable with Profil bindings (Equipe models with a groove for the second Pilot axle), but Profil boots not usable with Pilot bindings due to the wider guide ridge. Amer Sports offered SNS under Salomon and Atomic brands. In 2007, Fischer abandoned SNS and switched entirely to the NIS format of the NNN system. Rottefella's NNN binding has a bar in the boot toe hooked into a latch in the binding, offered in classical and skating, touring and racing configurations; second-generation bindings are not compatible with first-generation designs. A heavy-duty, wider version, NNN–BC, is designed for back-country skiing. The Nordic Integrated System (NIS), introduced in 2005 by Rossignol, Madshus, Rottefella, and Alpina, incorporates an NNN-compatible toe attachment into an integrated binding plate on the ski top, allowing field adjustment with a metallic NIS key; the initial design used a movable insert with a tool, later refined to allow binding position adjustment with a locking knob while wearing the skis; NIS skis allow installation of non-NIS bindings. In 2016, Fischer and Rossignol introduced an "integrated fixation plate" (IFP) binding allowing tool-less adjustment of NNN-compatible binding position. The Turnamic uses step-in locking with a lever that turns to open or close. In 2016, Salomon introduced its NNN-compatible Prolink system. In 2007, Rottefella introduced the New Telemark Norm binding with lateral release, adjustability, and a freely pivoting toe attachment. Ski jumping bindings attach to the toe of square-toed plastic boots that extend above the ankles, allowing the heel to rise and releasing in a fall.
